theoryAdd.text: Both combination rules come straight from Kirchhoff's laws. In series the single current I flows through every resistor, so KVL gives V = IR₁ + IR₂ + … = I(R₁ + R₂ + …), and the bracket is the series total. In parallel the common voltage V drives V/R₁, V/R₂, … through the branches, and KCL gives I = V(1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …), so the conductances add. Each extra series resistor adds another drop, and each extra parallel branch adds another path, which is why a series total always exceeds its largest member and a parallel equivalent always lies below its smallest.

theoryAdd.plainText: Three in parallel: Rp = R1 R2 R3 / (R1 R2 + R2 R3 + R3 R1)

theoryAdd.text:
Worked example 1 - ladder network, reduce from the far end
30 V supply -> 5 Ω in series -> node A; 20 Ω from A to the return line;
also from A: 6 Ω in series with 14 Ω to the return line
Far branch: 6 + 14 = 20 Ω
At A: 20 Ω || 20 Ω = 10 Ω
Total: R_eq = 5 + 10 = 15 Ω, so I = 30/15 = 2 A
V_A = 2 × 10 = 20 V; current in the 20 Ω shunt = 20/20 = 1 A; far branch = 1 A
V(14 Ω) = 14 V and V(6 Ω) = 6 V (check: 6 + 14 = 20 V = V_A)

Worked example 2 - a voltage divider under load
Unloaded: 12 V across R1 = 4 kΩ (top) and R2 = 2 kΩ (bottom)
V_out = 12 × 2/(4 + 2) = 4 V
Load R_L = 2 kΩ across R2: R2 || R_L = 1 kΩ
V_out = 12 × 1/(4 + 1) = 2.4 V (a 40 % fall)
Load R_L = 200 kΩ: R2 || R_L = 1.980 kΩ, V_out = 12 × 1.980/5.980 = 3.97 V
Rule: keep R_L at least 10 times, preferably 100 times, the lower divider resistor

Worked example 3 - lamps of different rating in series (resistance taken as constant)
Two 230 V lamps, 60 W and 100 W, in series across 230 V
R60 = 230²/60 = 881.7 Ω; R100 = 230²/100 = 529 Ω
I = 230/(881.7 + 529) = 0.163 A
P60 = 0.163² × 881.7 = 23.4 W; P100 = 0.163² × 529 = 14.1 W
In series the 60 W lamp glows brighter (same I, higher R);
in parallel across 230 V the 100 W lamp is brighter (same V, lower R)

rows: Divides; smallest R takes the most
Conductances add; less than the smallest

theoryAdd.text: When N identical cells are arranged in m parallel rows, each row having n cells in series (N = mn), the battery has EMF nE and internal resistance nr/m. The current in an external resistor R is nE/(R + nr/m), and for a fixed number of cells it is greatest when the arrangement makes the internal resistance equal to the external resistance, R = nr/m, which is the maximum power transfer condition in another form.

theoryAdd.plainText: I = nE / (R + nr/m) ;  maximum when R = nr/m

theoryAdd.text: Special cases shorten many problems. A resistor with a short circuit across it carries no current and can be deleted, and so can a resistor that leads only to an open end. In a balanced Wheatstone bridge (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄) the two midpoints are at the same potential, so the element bridging them carries no current and may be removed or shorted without changing anything. A uniform wire of resistance R cut into n equal pieces that are then joined in parallel gives R/n².

items: Using product-over-sum on three resistors at once; it is valid for exactly two.
Swapping resistances in the current-divider rule: the current in R₁ is I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Ignoring the load on a voltage divider: a load across the lower resistor always lowers the output.
Treating two resistors as series when a branch leaves the node between them; series requires the same current with no junction in between.
Assuming the higher-wattage lamp is always brighter: true in parallel, but in series the lower-wattage (higher-resistance) lamp dissipates more.
Forgetting internal resistance: n cells in series have nr, n identical cells in parallel have r/n.

theoryAdd.text: For power questions, pick the formula that holds the common quantity fixed: in series the current is common, so use P = I²R and the largest resistor dissipates most; in parallel the voltage is common, so use P = V²/R and the smallest resistor dissipates most.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series across a 40 V supply. The circuit current is:
An extra resistor is connected in series with an existing circuit across a fixed supply. The supply current:
questions.explanation: Adding a series resistor increases the total resistance, so I = V/R_total falls.

questions.questionText: The equivalent resistance of a 6 Ω resistor in parallel with a 12 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: R_p = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω, less than the smaller resistor as expected.

questions.questionText: Five identical resistors are connected first in series and then in parallel. The ratio R_series/R_parallel is:
questions.explanation: R_series = 5R and R_parallel = R/5, so the ratio is 5R ÷ (R/5) = 25 = n².

questions.questionText: Several resistors are connected in parallel across a fixed supply. The one that dissipates the most power is the resistor with the:
questions.explanation: All branches share the same voltage, so P = V²/R is greatest for the smallest R.

questions.questionText: A 24 V supply is connected across a 2 kΩ and a 6 kΩ resistor in series. The voltage across the 6 kΩ resistor is:
questions.explanation: V₆ = 24 × 6/(2 + 6) = 18 V; the larger resistor takes the larger share.

questions.questionText: A total current of 9 A enters a 3 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor connected in parallel. The current in the 3 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: I₃ = I × R_other/(R₁ + R₂) = 9 × 6/(3 + 6) = 6 A; swapping the resistances gives the wrong 3 A.

questions.questionText: Household appliances are connected in parallel across the supply mainly because:
options: The total current drawn is reduced
The same current flows through every appliance
Each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently
questions.explanation: In parallel every appliance sees the rated supply voltage, and switching or failure of one does not affect the others.

questions.questionText: A 2 Ω, a 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are all connected between the same two terminals A and B. The resistance measured between A and B is:
An unknown resistor R in series with a 10 Ω resistor draws 2 A from a 50 V supply. The value of R is:
A 60 W, 230 V lamp and a 100 W, 230 V lamp are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Which statement is correct?
options: The 100 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher rating
Both glow equally because the current is the same
The 100 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher resistance
The 60 W lamp glows brighter because it has the higher resistance
questions.explanation: The 60 W lamp has the higher resistance (V²/P = 882 Ω against 529 Ω); with the same current in series, P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp.

questions.questionText: Two resistors have an equivalent of 25 Ω in series and 4 Ω in parallel. Their values are:
questions.explanation: R₁ + R₂ = 25 and R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 4 give R₁R₂ = 100, so the values are the roots of x² − 25x + 100 = 0: 20 Ω and 5 Ω.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel across a 60 V supply. The total current drawn is:
questions.explanation: Branch currents are 60/10 = 6 A, 60/20 = 3 A and 60/30 = 2 A, totalling 11 A (1 A would be the series current).

questions.questionText: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel across a fixed supply and one of them burns out (goes open circuit). Then:
options: The other two also go out
The other two keep the same brightness and the supply current falls
questions.explanation: Each remaining lamp still has the full supply voltage, so its current and brightness are unchanged; only the burnt-out lamp's share of the supply current disappears.

questions.questionText: A 40 W, 220 V lamp and a 100 W, 220 V lamp are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Assuming constant lamp resistances, the power taken by the 40 W lamp is about:
questions.explanation: R₄₀ = 220²/40 = 1210 Ω and R₁₀₀ = 220²/100 = 484 Ω; I = 220/1694 = 0.130 A; P₄₀ = I²R₄₀ = 20.4 W (8.2 W is the 100 W lamp, 28.6 W the total).

questions.questionText: Ten identical lamps are connected in series across a fixed supply. If one lamp is short-circuited, the remaining nine lamps:
options: Glow dimmer, because the current falls
Glow brighter, because each gets a larger share of the supply voltage
questions.explanation: The total resistance falls from 10R to 9R, so the current rises and each remaining lamp's voltage rises from V/10 to V/9.

questions.questionText: A 100 V supply feeds two 10 kΩ resistors in series. A 10 kΩ load is connected across the lower resistor. The voltage across the load is about:
questions.explanation: 10 kΩ || 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ, so V_load = 100 × 5/(10 + 5) = 33.3 V; the unloaded divider would give 50 V.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a parallel circuit is NOT correct?
options: The equivalent resistance is greater than the largest branch resistance
The branch with the smallest resistance carries the largest current
The total conductance equals the sum of the branch conductances
Every branch has the same voltage across it
questions.explanation: Adding parallel paths lowers the resistance, so the equivalent is always less than the smallest branch; the other statements are true.

questions.questionText: A 2 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of a 6 Ω resistor and a branch of two 3 Ω resistors in series. The network is connected to 20 V. The current in the 6 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: The 3 + 3 = 6 Ω branch in parallel with 6 Ω gives 3 Ω; total 2 + 3 = 5 Ω, so I = 20/5 = 4 A, which splits equally between the two 6 Ω paths: 2 A.

questions.questionText: What resistance must be connected in parallel with a 30 Ω resistor to give an equivalent of 12 Ω?
questions.explanation: 1/R = 1/12 − 1/30 = (5 − 2)/60 = 1/20, so R = 20 Ω (18 Ω is the simple difference, which is wrong for parallel).

questions.questionText: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the element connected between the two midpoints of the bridge:
options: Carries no current and can be removed or shorted without changing the equivalent resistance
Must be replaced by a short circuit, otherwise the equivalent resistance is wrong
questions.explanation: At balance the two midpoints are at the same potential, so no current flows through the bridging element; removing it or shorting it gives the same equivalent resistance.

questions.questionText: n identical resistors of resistance R give 2 Ω in parallel and 50 Ω in series. Then:
questions.explanation: nR = 50 and R/n = 2; dividing gives n² = 25, so n = 5 and R = 10 Ω.

questions.questionText: A uniform wire of resistance R is cut into four equal pieces, and the pieces are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:
questions.explanation: Each piece has R/4; four of them in parallel give (R/4)/4 = R/16.

questions.questionText: An ammeter is connected ____ with the load and should have a ____ resistance.
questions.explanation: The ammeter must carry the load current, so it goes in series, and its resistance must be very low so it does not reduce that current.

questions.questionText: A uniform wire of resistance 16 Ω is bent into a circle. The resistance between two points on the circle separated by a quarter of the circumference is:
questions.explanation: The two arcs are 4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel: (4 × 12)/(4 + 12) = 3 Ω (4 Ω would be for diametrically opposite points).

questions.questionText: Six cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are connected in series to a 7 Ω load. The terminal voltage of the battery is:
A 12 V battery and a 10 V battery, each with a small internal resistance, are connected in parallel with no load. What happens?
options: No current flows because there is no load
Each battery keeps its own terminal voltage and no current flows
A large circulating current flows from the 12 V battery into the 10 V battery
questions.explanation: The 2 V difference drives a current limited only by the two small internal resistances, discharging one battery into the other; this is why cells of unequal EMF are not paralleled.

questions.questionText: Four identical cells, each of EMF 2 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω, are connected in parallel to a 1.9 Ω load. The load current is:
questions.explanation: In parallel E = 2 V and r = 0.4/4 = 0.1 Ω, so I = 2/(1.9 + 0.1) = 1 A (0.87 A results from forgetting to divide r by 4).

questions.questionText: Identical cells are connected in parallel rather than in series mainly to:
options: Increase the current capacity while keeping the EMF of one cell
questions.explanation: Parallel cells keep the EMF of one cell but divide the internal resistance by n and add their ampere-hour capacities.

questions.questionText: Twelve cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.6 Ω, are arranged in 3 parallel rows of 4 cells in series. The current in an external 2 Ω resistor is about:
questions.explanation: Each row has E = 4 × 1.5 = 6 V and r = 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 Ω; three rows in parallel give 6 V and 0.8 Ω, so I = 6/(2 + 0.8) = 2.14 A.

questions.questionText: Resistors of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are in parallel across a battery. A wire of negligible resistance is accidentally connected across the 30 Ω resistor. The equivalent resistance becomes:
options: 6.67 Ω, the value of 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel
Zero, so the battery is short-circuited
questions.explanation: The wire is a 0 Ω branch in parallel with everything, and a parallel equivalent cannot exceed its smallest branch, so the whole combination becomes 0 Ω.

questions.questionText: Sixteen identical cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are to deliver the maximum current to an external 4 Ω resistor. The best arrangement is:
options: 4 parallel rows of 4 cells in series
8 parallel rows of 2 cells in series
2 parallel rows of 8 cells in series
questions.explanation: Maximum current needs nr/m = R with nm = 16: n/m = 4 gives n = 8, m = 2, so I = 12/(4 + 4) = 1.5 A, more than the 1.2 A given by 4 rows of 4 or by 16 cells in series.

questions.questionText: The rule that the total current in a parallel circuit equals the sum of the branch currents follows directly from:
questions.explanation: KCL states that the current entering a node equals the current leaving it, so the supply current equals the sum of the branch currents.

questions.questionText: A 10 Ω and a 40 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 20 V supply. The total power dissipated is:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R₁ + V²/R₂ = 400/10 + 400/40 = 40 + 10 = 50 W (8 W would be the series case).

questions.questionText: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are in series across a 20 V supply. The power dissipated in the 5 Ω resistor is:
questions.explanation: I = 20/10 = 2 A, so P₅ = I²R = 4 × 5 = 20 W (80 W wrongly applies the full 20 V to the 5 Ω resistor).

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, the largest voltage drop appears across the:
questions.explanation: The same current flows through all, so each drop IR is proportional to the resistance.

questions.questionText: A resistor R is connected in parallel with a 6 Ω resistor, and this combination is in series with a 4 Ω resistor. The total resistance is 8 Ω. The value of R is:
questions.explanation: The parallel pair must equal 8 − 4 = 4 Ω, so 1/R = 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 and R = 12 Ω.

questions.questionText: To keep the output of a voltage divider close to its unloaded value when a load is connected, the load resistance should be:
options: Much smaller than the divider resistors
Equal to the lower divider resistor
Much larger than the divider resistors
questions.explanation: A load in parallel with the lower resistor lowers the effective resistance and the output; the effect is negligible only when the load is much larger (10 to 100 times) than that resistor.

questions.questionText: A meter movement of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The shunt needed to make it an ammeter reading 1 A full scale is about:
questions.explanation: The shunt carries 1 − 0.001 = 0.999 A at the same voltage as the meter (0.001 × 50 = 0.05 V), so R_sh = 0.05/0.999 = 0.050 Ω.

questions.questionText: A fuse is connected in series with the circuit it protects because:
options: It must have the full supply voltage across it
It raises the total resistance to limit the current
A series connection lowers its melting point
The whole circuit current passes through it, so it can interrupt that current when it melts
questions.explanation: Only a series element carries the full circuit current; when that current is excessive the fuse element melts and opens the one path the current has.

questions.questionText: A meter movement of resistance 500 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The series resistance needed to make it a 0 to 5 V voltmeter is:
questions.explanation: Total resistance = 5/0.001 = 5000 Ω, so the series multiplier = 5000 − 500 = 4500 Ω (5000 Ω forgets the meter's own resistance).

questions.questionText: A 6 V, 0.3 A lamp is to be run from a 12 V supply. The resistance to be connected in series with it is:
questions.explanation: The resistor must drop 12 − 6 = 6 V at 0.3 A: R = 6/0.3 = 20 Ω (40 Ω is the total circuit resistance).

questions.questionText: A bridge has arms of 2 Ω and 4 Ω in one path and 3 Ω and 6 Ω in the other, with a 10 Ω resistor connecting the two midpoints. The equivalent resistance between the supply terminals is:
questions.explanation: 2/4 = 3/6, so the bridge is balanced and the 10 Ω carries no current; R = (2 + 4) || (3 + 6) = (6 × 9)/15 = 3.6 Ω.

questions.questionText: Two resistors with conductances of 0.2 S and 0.3 S are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation: Conductances add in parallel: G = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5 S, so R = 1/G = 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: The terminal voltage of a battery delivering current is less than its EMF because of:
options: The voltage drop across its internal resistance
The power factor of the load
The insulation resistance of the leads
questions.explanation: V = E − Ir: part of the EMF is used up driving the current through the battery's own internal resistance.

questions.questionText: Two 12 Ω resistors in series draw 1 A from a 24 V supply. A third 12 Ω resistor is then connected in parallel with one of them. The new supply current is:
questions.explanation: The parallel pair is 6 Ω, so R = 12 + 6 = 18 Ω and I = 24/18 = 1.33 A; the current rises because the total resistance fell.
